lines: Every structure from here back answered one question: is this key here, and where. This chapter asks something different about an array that keeps changing.
What's true about a stretch of positions, right now, while individual positions keep getting updated underneath you.
Scan the stretch for an answer and the cost grows with how many positions there are. Cache a running total instead, and an update just moves that same cost somewhere else.
Here's the one piece of arithmetic the whole chapter runs on.
Every index owns a range of the array, and that range is set entirely by the index's own lowest set bit, the rightmost one bit in its binary form.
An index ending in a single one bit owns a short range of its own. An index that is a clean power of two owns almost everything beneath it.
Before the reveal, a natural first guess is that fixing one position after a change means touching everything downstream of it.
Ask instead how far an update actually has to walk, if it only ever jumps by its own lowest set bit.
answer: Each jump adds the current index's own lowest set bit, and the walk runs past the end of the array after only a few jumps.
Doubling the array's size would only add one more jump, not many more positions touched.

lines: Watch the jumps land: a direct arithmetic walk, not a tree being climbed one node at a time.
A short handful of positions touched, forward, each one found by adding the previous index's own lowest set bit.
Before this reveal, notice the query runs the identical arithmetic in reverse, subtracting a lowest set bit instead of adding one.
Does that reverse walk take the same number of jumps the update did, or a different number entirely?
answer: The same count turns up here, but that's a property of these two particular positions, not a rule that an update and a query always match.
Pick a different starting position and the two counts can easily come apart.

lines: Same arithmetic, opposite direction: each jump now subtracts the current index's own lowest set bit instead of adding it.
A short handful of positions visited, and their own stored partial sums add straight up to the running total.
A stretch between two positions is just one running total subtracted from another, nothing new to compute, only a difference to take.
The same pairing trick, run on two separate trees instead of one, turns a single update into a correction applied across an entire stretch at once.
Before this reveal, resist the pull toward assuming a grid needs something smarter than the one-dimensional trick.
Ask plainly whether running the identical jump arithmetic once along each axis actually works, or whether a second dimension breaks it.
answer: It works, nested exactly that way: the same jump arithmetic, run once along each axis in turn.
Nothing about the underlying bit trick changes. Only how many times it gets applied.

lines: Two nested walks, one per axis, and the structure composes without needing any new idea.
The measured total here was checked directly against summing every cell by hand, not assumed from the one-dimensional case.
Here's where every claimed saving gets checked against a real count instead of an argument.
Across the same batch of updates and lookups on the identical array, a naive cached running total touched far more positions in total than the Fenwick tree's own jumps did.
